title: Barkman Avenue rebuilt as a local improvement (Main to Henry Street)
summary: Council used a local improvement plan (LIP 2016-01, By-law 2060) to rebuild about three blocks of Barkman Avenue, one of Steinbach's older streets: surface works, water main and sewer main. About half was borrowed over five years and most of the rest came from federal and provincial grants. One objection was registered. Council saw it as part of a planned, long-term renewal of older streets.
status_detail: First and second reading Dec 15, 2015. The Municipal Board approved the borrowing and third reading was given Feb 16, 2016. Construction was part of the 2016 capital works tender ($2.955M to Maple Leaf Construction, Mar 15, 2016).
figures: Total $2.14M; $1M borrowed over 5 years; $840,000 Canada-Manitoba Infrastructure Program; $300,000 Municipal Road Improvement program (transcript 2015-12-15 0:06:22). 2016 capital works tender $2.955M including Barkman, pavement management and sidewalks (transcript 2016-03-15 0:05:40). Related: Elmdale/Lumber local improvement debenture $2.145M at 2.4% over 5 years (transcript 2015-12-15 0:12:41; 2016-02-02 1:15:14).
reasons: already-planned: Part of a long-term strategy to renew underground infrastructure before it fails. (Chris Goertzen); cost: Mostly paid by other governments; already in the budget, so no tax-rate effect. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: One registered objection (contents not read out); no one spoke at the Dec 15, 2015 hearing.
notes: Barkman first-reading mover was transcribed 'Councilor Swiper'; Zwaagstra is the likely mover. Which Councillor Penner seconded is not stated.

title: Home Street North drainage swale: residents' petition; fix judged too costly
summary: Residents of Home Street North asked council to replace an open drainage swale that sends water and ice across the street (an area the city took over from Hanover decades ago). Council asked for a report in Dec 2015 and, after a delegation and petition in Feb 2017, passed a motion for costed options. In Dec 2017 the City Manager reported that a culvert or bridge crossing would cost about $500,000 plus property purchases, so the city would only monitor and maintain the crossing until the street is someday rebuilt.
status_detail: Dec 5, 2017: no reconstruction; extra monitoring and maintenance continue; reconfiguration only 'in the relatively distant future' when the street is due for reconstruction. The Mayor asked that the residents be told the cost.
figures: Piped crossing/bridge estimated about $500,000 plus property purchases (transcript 2017-12-05 1:24:16); Mayor summarised it as 'over $1 million' (1:27:59). Mid-1990s review found the road would need to be raised about 1 m (transcript 2017-02-07 0:19:46).
reasons: cost: A culvert/bridge crossing would be extremely costly and require buying property. (Troy Warkentin); standards-met: Swales are common in older areas (Fairmount, Barkman, Creekside, Giesbrecht); public works gives the spot extra attention. (Troy Warkentin); wait-for-development: Fix could be considered when the street is reconstructed in future; not on any capital plan. (Troy Warkentin)
public: K.B., a Home Street resident, wrote in Dec 2015 and presented a petition in Feb 2017: water and ice across the road for weeks after rain, vehicles damaged, pedestrians forced to walk through water, and residents paying for sidewalks they don't have (residents' claims). He warned of liability if someone is hurt. In Aug 2018 he objected to a nearby rezoning over added runoff to the swale.
vote: carried (Feb 7, 2017 motion for a costed options report); Dec 2017 report received, no action
notes: Which Councillor Penner moved the Feb 7, 2017 motion cannot be determined (the other Penner was also present). Petition contents and signature count not in the transcript.

title: Request for a sidewalk/pathway along Old Tom Road deferred to the sidewalk plan
summary: Residents on Lyons Gate wrote asking that a sidewalk be built with the Old Tom Road paving. Staff said their own estimate ($700,000-$800,000) would roughly double the project. Council kept paving and sidewalks separate: the request would be considered in the overall sidewalk plan, and the Mayor pointed to regional pathways once annexed land east of the road joined the city.
status_detail: No motion; referred in discussion to future sidewalk/pathway planning. No sidewalk on Old Tom Road found in this period; the related Clearspring Greens walking-access request returned in June 2018 (see 2018-clearspring-greens-pathway).
figures: Sidewalk estimate $700,000-$800,000 (residents' figure, per transcript 2016-02-02 1:19:50); $1M budgeted for the paving.
reasons: cost: Would add $700k-$800k to a $1M project. (Troy Warkentin); study-first: Separate discussion; focus on the roadway first, then a bigger consultation. (Jac Siemens); wait-for-development: Annexation of land east of the road could open pathway options later. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Residents on Lyons Gate (surname initial T.) asked for a sidewalk with the paving.
vote: no motion; consensus to consider in sidewalk plan
notes: A councillor (unnamed in the transcript, speaker K at 1:20:44) cautioned against making sidewalks automatic with boundary-road paving because it would slow paving of other boundary roads; likely Zwaagstra but not confirmed.

title: Runoff on low lots near Old Tom Road and through the golf course creek
summary: A resident at Lowen Boulevard and Old Tom Road wrote (again) about water on his low-lying lot. Staff said the drain is provincial and city improvements happen only when development prompts them. In July 2016 the Steinbach Fly-In Golf Club said development in and around the city was sending more water through the course and asked for a partnership and compensation; the Mayor confirmed new subdivisions must keep 'net zero' outflow, as the province requires.
status_detail: No city works decided. Deputy Mayor Fehr said the conservation district was in talks with the golf course to manage water downstream first. The golf club's requests were not acted on in this item (the city later dealt with the golf course property in Dec 2017, outside this topic).
figures: Golf club estimated about $48,000/yr in lost revenue from closures (delegate, transcript 2016-07-05 0:35:12).
reasons: wait-for-development: Improvements to significant drains are initiated by developer prompt; none planned there. (Troy Warkentin); private-property: Low lots on the original creek bed; drain under provincial jurisdiction. (Troy Warkentin); standards-met: New subdivisions already must hold outflow to pre-development levels (net zero). (Chris Goertzen)
public: R.F. (resident) letter on drainage at his property (not his first). Steinbach Fly-In Golf Club (rep J.S.) asked for a partnership, compensation and future funding, saying more water arrives than ever and that properties at Lowen and Old Tom flood (delegate's claim).
notes: Golf club's figures and claims are the delegate's and were not verified.

title: Old Tom Road (boundary road) paved at full scope despite tender over budget
summary: Old Tom Road, a boundary road on the city's edge that residents had long complained about, came in about $200,000 over its $1M budget. Staff proposed cutting the scope; council tabled it on Apr 5, 2016, then on May 3 approved the full tender, covering the gap from surplus or the capital development reserve.
status_detail: Full tender awarded to Bituminex Paving on May 3, 2016, extra ~$200,000 from year-end surplus or the capital development reserve.
figures: Low tender $1,058,417 plus ~$140,000 engineering vs $1M budget (transcript 2016-04-05_part2 0:23:44); extra about $200,000; CDR would fall to about $500,000 (transcript 2016-05-03 0:04:37).
reasons: cost: Delaying would only raise costs. (John Fehr); already-planned: Long overdue, already delayed before; should not cut scope. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Residents near the road had complained about its condition for years (as reported by Zwaagstra).

title: One-time exception lets a developer use swale drainage instead of curb and gutter (Steinbach North, C-3)
summary: Steinbach Land Holding Partners asked to convert its approved bare-land condo (low-pressure sewer, 24-ft asphalt, swales) to a regular subdivision with gravity sewer, piped water and 32-ft concrete streets, but keep open swale drainage with no curb and gutter. Staff said it lowered the urban standard toward a 'rural profile' and would set a precedent for all developers. After deferring it on Apr 5, council approved it on May 3, 2016 through the development agreement as a one-time exception.
status_detail: Approved May 3, 2016 'through development agreement, one-time ask for this development' (gravity sewer, piped water, 32-ft concrete street, swale drainage, no concrete curb and gutter). Mayor Goertzen did not take part (declared a perceived conflict regarding Northview Development).
figures: Street width 32 ft vs 24 ft at Hespeler Industrial Park; developer claimed ~$800,000/yr in added taxes at build-out (developer's claim, transcript 2016-05-03 0:10:18); city spec manual ~150 pages (0:26:15).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Not a variance; changes the spec and every similar developer would expect the same. (Michael Zwaagstra); standards-met: City spec (curb, landscaped boulevards, land drainage sewer) applies consistently; this is a lower 'rural profile'. (Troy Warkentin); cost: Private developer paying, attracts business and jobs; swales work elsewhere. (Jac Siemens)
public: Developer representatives (D.C. and B.S., for Steinbach Land Holding Partners / Northview Developments) said city condo conditions erased their savings, buyers resisted condo fees, and the city's specs priced private developers out (developer's claims).
vote: carried; count not recorded (Zwaagstra stated he would vote against)
notes: Speaker labels in the Apr 5 and May 3 videos merge some councillors with the developer's representatives; only turns with a named call right before are attributed. The resolution text is as read out at 0:36:43 (no minutes for 2016).

title: New subdivisions on annexed land approved subject to development agreements
summary: Council approved successive phases of the Lexington Village development off McKenzie Avenue (on land annexed from Hanover in 2014) and the next Harmony Lane/Prairie Crescent phase, each 'subject to the prior execution of a development agreement'. Servicing terms (sidewalks, grading, parks, timing, securities) were not discussed at the table; members spoke about growth and lot supply.
status_detail: Jul 19, 2016: Crescentwood Dr extension, Lincoln and Nicolette Ave (phase 2). Feb 20, 2018: 71 lots, Alexander Way, Imperial Crescent, Acorn Ave (R18-031). Jun 5, 2018: rezoning By-law 2094 aligning the plan. Jul 3, 2018: Prairie Homes subdivision and Prairie Crescent (R18-154).
figures: Phase 2 (2016): 32 single-family, 3 low-density, 2 medium-density lots (transcript 2016-07-19 1:08:27); phase 3 (2018): 71 lots (R18-031). 2017: just over 100 new residential lots approved city-wide (City Manager, transcript 2018-02-06 0:04:58).
reasons: developer-pays: Approvals conditional on development agreements negotiated by staff. (Council)
public: No objections at the 2016 and Feb 2018 hearings; one late letter on the Jul 2018 subdivision (L.R.) about lot reconfiguration.
notes: Routine approvals grouped. Development agreement contents are not in the transcripts or minutes reviewed.

title: Lot-line subdivision at 275 Third Street: staff urged denial over drainage; tie vote, then tabled
summary: Two neighbours in an established area asked to move a lot line (275 Third Street / 4 Fernwood Bay). Staff recommended denial because of drainage patterns and future servicing, or else a professional lot-grading plan for all six surrounding lots. A motion to deny tied and failed; council then tabled the file.
status_detail: Motion to deny lost on a tie (Siemens absent); file tabled to the next meeting. No later decision found in the 2016 transcripts.
reasons: private-property: City can't impose grading conditions on neighbouring private lots; neighbours usually work it out. (Troy Warkentin); standards-met: Follow the engineer's advice so future owners avoid drainage problems. (Councillor Penner (mover; which Penner unclear))
public: The applicants (two neighbouring owners) supplied extra material; no public hearing.
mover: Councillor Penner (deny; which Penner not determinable)
vote: tie, motion to deny lost; then tabled (moved Zwaagstra, seconded Penner)
notes: With six members present the tie was 3-3; the transcript does not record every vote. Which Councillor Penner moved denial is unclear.

title: Council refuses to waive a drainage-plan condition for an owner in an older area
summary: A homeowner whose variance (for a large shed) was conditional on a drainage plan wrote asking for relief from the $2,000-$3,000 cost. Staff said the city-wide drainage policy (15-20 years old) applies to all development and helps fix older areas lot by lot. Council kept the policy.
status_detail: No motion; the Mayor directed staff to tell the owner 'that the policy stands'.
figures: Drainage plan cost $2,000-$3,000 (Mayor, transcript 2016-09-20 0:23:54).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Waiving it would undo the policy; fix older areas one lot at a time. (Earl Funk); standards-met: Engineered plans protect neighbours and shift responsibility to engineers. (John Fehr)
public: R.C. (resident; had the variance approved in July 2016 with neighbours' support) asked for relief from the cost.

title: Albert Street residents ask for a sidewalk; report requested, no sidewalk built
summary: An Albert Street resident wrote that traffic had grown and asked for a sidewalk. Staff said established neighbourhoods historically got sidewalks on a 50/50 basis: half paid by benefiting owners, half city debt. Council passed a motion for a report on cost and background for the 2017 budget. The issue came up again in 2017 when a seniors' complex was approved next door.
status_detail: Report motion carried Oct 4, 2016. No report or sidewalk decision found in later transcripts; in Aug 2017 Siemens asked that it go back on the study-session agenda.
figures: Historic formula: 50% benefiting owners, 50% city-wide debt (transcript 2016-10-04 0:20:10).
reasons: residents-pay-local-improvement: Older-area sidewalks follow the 50/50 owner/city formula. (Troy Warkentin); study-first: Get information and gauge support, since owners may pay. (Michael Zwaagstra); already-planned: A creek pathway one block over gives another route; monitor. (John Fehr)
public: T.M. (resident) wrote asking for a sidewalk and offered to canvass neighbours. In July 2017 A.M., another Albert Street resident, asked at a hearing whether a sidewalk was planned.
notes: Study sessions are closed; any decision there is not in the public record reviewed.

title: Development fees renewed to 2019, including the sidewalk levy for new neighbourhoods
summary: Council renewed the residential (By-law 2070) and non-residential (By-law 2071) capital development fees for 2017-2019 with 2.5% yearly increases. Councillors explained that the residential fee includes a sidewalk levy, so new neighbourhoods get sidewalks paid by the fee, while established streets without sidewalks still rely on other funding.
status_detail: First reading Oct 4, 2016; second and third reading Nov 1, 2016.
figures: 2.5% per year, 3-year schedule to end of 2019 (transcript 2016-10-04 0:09:24, 0:11:07).
reasons: developer-pays: New developments should pay toward the impact on the city, including new sidewalks. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (2070 first reading); John Fehr (2071)
notes: Fee amounts per unit were not read out.

title: New sidewalk on Clearwater Avenue, with a provincial grant application
summary: Council applied to the provincial Small Communities Transportation Fund for $50,000 toward a 500-metre sidewalk on Clearwater Avenue (estimated $185,000), used by students walking to school. The project was part of the 2017 capital works tender.
status_detail: Grant application approved Feb 7, 2017; 2017 capital works tender awarded Mar 7, 2017 included Clearwater. Grant outcome not found.

title: Playground renewal in established parks with provincial grants (Chote Park, Giesbrecht Park)
summary: The city has a playground renewal program for older parks. When the provincial Community Places Program reopened, council applied for about $10,000 for Chote Park (granted $10,557) and in 2018 up to $12,000 for Giesbrecht Park playground equipment (granted).
status_detail: Chote Park application Sep 5, 2017; grant of $10,557 reported Nov 21, 2017. Giesbrecht Park application R18-117 (May 15, 2018); grant announcement received Aug 7, 2018.
figures: Chote Park grant $10,557 (transcript 2017-11-21 0:32:59); Giesbrecht Park up to $12,000 (R18-117).
notes: No discussion of playgrounds or park development in new subdivisions was found in this period.

title: Annexation from Hanover: planning grant, 11 miles of gravel roads and services added
summary: After the Municipal Board report on the city's annexation application, council applied for a provincial grant to rewrite its plan and zoning for the new land. In Feb 2018 the City Manager reported just under 3,000 acres and about 11 miles of gravel roads were added, and that public works and solid waste had folded the area into their service plans without difficulty. Canada Post planned to move the added homes to community mailboxes, so council renamed annexed roads in Aug 2018.
status_detail: Planning grant application approved Sep 19, 2017; annexation approved by the province (less than requested); emergency plan updated (R18-028); road renaming by-law passed second and third reading Aug 21, 2018.
figures: Just under 3,000 acres; about 11 miles of gravel roads (transcript 2018-02-06 0:04:58); grant up to 50% of review cost (2017-09-19 0:17:41).
reasons: study-first: New land needs proper city standards and designations through the plan review. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: City Manager said annexed-area residents were kept informed and comments were 'generally... very positive' (staff characterisation).
notes: No transcript discussion of garbage service levels, wells or road upgrades for specific annexed properties was found beyond these reports.

title: Businesses on gravel roads no longer required to pave parking (Park Road West cases; Zoning By-law 2100)
summary: Businesses on gravel roads, such as on Park Road West, asked to be excused from paving required parking. Council granted a Dec 2017 variance to a tool-rental business despite an outstanding work order. In the new zoning by-law it chose (4-2) to require only an all-weather surface where a site abuts an unpaved road, and in Oct 2018 approved (6-1) another Park Road West variance. Supporters cited cost and the city's own gravel yard; the Mayor and Cari Penner defended paving standards and signed agreements.
status_detail: Dec 5, 2017 variance carried (count not recorded); Jun 5, 2018 surfacing option 2 adopted (R18-128, 4-2) and kept in By-law 2100 (third reading Oct 16, 2018); Oct 2, 2018 V-2018-24 approved (R18-234, 6-1).
reasons: cost: Asphalt is expensive for start-ups on lower-value gravel-road land. (John Fehr); fairness-precedent: Like for like: the city gives gravel roads, so it shouldn't demand more. (Earl Funk); standards-met: Against: high urban standards serve the city when roads are later paved. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Owners/agents for a Park Road West tool-rental business (Dec 2017) and for 266 Park Road West (Oct 2018) said they were not told paving was required (applicants' claims); staff said paving was a condition of the 2015 permits.
vote: R18-128 4-2 (against: Goertzen, C. Penner); R18-234 6-1 (against: C. Penner)
notes: Commercial site standard rather than a neighbourhood service, included because it sets the paving standard on unpaved (largely fringe/annexed) roads. The Dec 2017 mover is 'Councilor Penner' (likely Susan Penner, not confirmed).

title: McKenzie Avenue rebuilt in concrete as a local improvement
summary: Council initiated and passed Local Improvement Plan 2018-02 (By-law 2090) to rebuild part of McKenzie Avenue near Brandt Street in concrete because of heavy truck traffic. $500,000 was borrowed over five years and levied on all taxpayers, with the rest from the capital development reserve and a benefiting property owner. A provincial road-program grant was also sought.
status_detail: Initiated Nov 21, 2017; hearing and second reading Dec 19, 2017 (no objectors); third reading Feb 20, 2018 (R18-035); tender $514,410 to Maple Leaf Construction (R18-060, Mar 20, 2018); MRIP request $400,000 for McKenzie and Hespeler St N (R18-157, Jul 3, 2018).
figures: Total $810,000; borrowing up to $500,000 over 5 years levied city-wide (transcript 2017-12-19 0:09:49); 210 m of roadway (2017-11-21 0:21:18); tender $514,410 (R18-060).
reasons: already-planned: Part of the regular renewal program. (Councillor Penner (which Penner not determinable))
public: No objections at the Dec 19, 2017 hearing.
notes: Nov 21 transcript says Lilac Bay to Highway 12; the by-law hearing and R18-060 say Lilac Bay to Brandt Street. The benefiting owner is not named (Barkman Concrete is mentioned as the truck generator).

title: 2018 neighbourhood sidewalk program builds sidewalks in newer neighbourhoods
summary: Council asked the province for $50,000 toward the 2018 neighbourhood sidewalk program (Lyndhurst Gate, Brighton Lane, Park Hill Crescent, Kroeker Avenue) and awarded a combined pavement-management and sidewalk tender. The province later said the city would not receive the grant.
status_detail: R18-040 grant request (Feb 20); R18-046 tender to Maple Leaf Construction (Mar 6). Aug 7, 2018 minutes: no funding under the 2018 Small Communities Transportation Fund.
figures: Grant request $50,000 (R18-040); tender $598,658 plus taxes (R18-046; transcript 2018-03-06 0:55:56).
reasons: developer-pays: New neighbourhoods get sidewalks after build-out, funded largely by the sidewalk levy. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Homeowners ask to move a new sidewalk away from their house; council leaves it per standard
summary: Owners of a corner lot on Lyndhurst Gate supported the new Brighton Lane sidewalk but asked that it be moved toward the curb because it would run close to their house. The city engineer said it followed the standard construction specification (in place since 1989) and that the developer had obtained a reduced 5-ft side yard, which created the squeeze. Council took no action. A month later Fehr asked whether council knows where sidewalks will go when it approves subdivisions; the City Manager said sidewalks funded by development fees are usually built only when a subdivision is 75-80% complete.
status_detail: No motion; contract already awarded; the sidewalk proceeded per spec. Funk asked staff to help with the owners' landscaping; Siemens objected that council had no report beforehand.
figures: Sidewalk planned 5 ft wide, 1 ft from the property line (delegate, transcript 2018-05-01 1:22:38); side yard varied from 8 ft to 5 ft at the developer's request (city engineer, 1:32:48).
reasons: standards-met: Standard spec puts sidewalks as far from traffic as possible and keeps utilities in fixed places. (City Engineer Phil Kalyta); cost: Contract already awarded; moving it would add cost (Penner not identifiable). (Councillor Penner); private-property: The variance was the developer's; buyers may not have been told. (John Fehr)
public: B.H. and his spouse (residents) asked to move the sidewalk closer to the curb and mailboxes, saying the developer's side-yard variance put it close to their home; they had met the engineer and City Manager first.
notes: Delegate identified by initials from the minutes (B.H.). Speaker O/K labels mix the engineer and delegate in places; only clearly engineer turns are used.

title: New plan and zoning for annexed land: farming can continue; septic fields replaceable only in Development Reserve 2
summary: Council adopted a new Official Community Plan (By-law 2099) and Zoning By-law 2100 mainly to cover the annexed land. A new Development Reserve 2 designation lets existing rural uses continue; on-site septic fields may be repaired or replaced only in that area, elsewhere a failing field means connecting to city sewer or a holding tank. Members credited staff for working with annexed-area residents at open houses.
status_detail: OCP first reading May 15, hearing and second reading Jul 17, ministerial approval, third reading Oct 16, 2018 (R18-242). Zoning By-law 2100 first reading Jun 5 (R18-129), third reading Oct 16 (R18-243).
reasons: standards-met: Policies 3.3.1-3.3.3 limit septic replacement to DR2. (Troy Warkentin); wait-for-development: Farmers in the reserve areas can keep farming until development comes. (Chris Goertzen)
public: At the Jul 17 hearing M.R. (farmer, northwest of the city) raised farmland loss and infill; T.B. (resident) urged waiting until after the election (residents' views).

title: Clearspring Greens residents ask for a sidewalk/pathway link; referred to study session
summary: A Mooney Avenue resident asked what was planned for Clearspring Greens and asked for a sidewalk and walking paths. Siemens said the area had no safe walking or cycling link except along Old Tom Road or Park Road, an issue since the subdivision was built. Council referred it to the July 2018 study session; the Mayor recalled a 'fairly hefty price tag' for earlier options.
status_detail: R18-130 referred to the July 2018 study session (closed). No public decision found before the Oct 2018 election.
reasons: cost: Earlier options had a 'fairly hefty price tag'. (Chris Goertzen); study-first: Discuss at study session; route may cross the golf course. (Jac Siemens)
public: S.D. (resident, Mooney Avenue) asked for a sidewalk and walking pathways.
notes: Clearspring Greens is a golf-course subdivision on the city's edge (Old Tom Road / Park Road).

title: Neighbours ask to remove a walkway on public reserve; council keeps it and turns to RCMP and school
summary: Residents of Cottonwood Bend asked the city to remove the sidewalk on public reserve between McKenzie Avenue and Cottonwood, citing vandalism, threats and loitering by students. Council asked for a report; staff recommended neither removing nor closing it (buried infrastructure needs access, and an earlier 2004 dispute was resolved through RCMP and school efforts). Council agreed by consensus to urge RCMP reporting, write to Hanover School Division and involve Citizens on Patrol.
status_detail: Removal declined Jul 17, 2018; consensus on RCMP/Citizens on Patrol/school-division follow-up.
figures: About a dozen incidents over five years (City Manager, transcript 2018-07-17 1:48:48).
reasons: standards-met: Removal not recommended; past problems were solved by RCMP/school cooperation. (Troy Warkentin); already-planned: Closing it gives no guarantee and the city wants more pathways, not fewer. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: P.F. and M.F. (residents) wrote asking for removal; a petition dated Jul 10, 2018 followed. A resident at the June meeting said 'we've heard that before'.
vote: unanimous (report by end of July); Jul 17 consensus

title: Hespeler Street South: variance approved on condition the septic field passes inspection; no city sewer on the street
summary: An owner on Hespeler Street South (zoned agricultural, 6.4 acres) needed a variance to add to the home. Council approved it subject to a licensed septic-field inspection. Staff explained that a working field may continue, but a failing one cannot be replaced: the owner must connect to city sewer or install a holding tank, and city sewer does not run down that part of Hespeler.
status_detail: R18-203 carried unanimously Sep 4, 2018. The owner's question about waiting until the whole street is serviced was answered with the policy; no sewer extension was discussed.
figures: Site 6.4 acres vs 20-acre minimum in the A zone (transcript 2018-09-04 0:07:42).
reasons: standards-met: OCP policy bars replacing septic fields; holding tank or city sewer instead. (Troy Warkentin)
public: The owner (J.M.) asked whether everyone along Hespeler would be required to connect and whether it would be more prudent to wait until all are connected.
notes: Owner's name differs between transcript and minutes; minutes used for initials.

title: Harmony Lane: part of a public reserve (green space) closed and reconfigured over neighbours' objections, 4-3
summary: A new ownership group took over a subdivision and asked to close and reconfigure part of the public reserve so new lots would need fewer variances. Two recent buyers on Chrysler Gate objected that they had checked city maps and been told the green space behind them would stay. Council approved second reading 4-3; supporters said fewer variances means better planning, opponents said the hearing should respect residents who did their homework.
status_detail: First reading Sep 18 (R18-220, unanimous); second reading Oct 16, 2018 (R18-249, 4-3); third reading needed ministerial approval (after this council's term).
figures: Reconfiguration moves lot lines about 10 feet into the reserve behind the objectors (transcript 2018-10-16 0:13:09, 0:21:18).
reasons: standards-met: Fewer variances is better long-term planning; subdivision already conditionally approved. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Against: residents relied on city maps; the hearing is their only voice. (Jac Siemens, Earl Funk, John Fehr)
public: G.D. and K.A. (residents of Chrysler Gate) objected: G.D. said the green-space access influenced the purchase and the seller and city maps showed it (residents' claims). The applicant's representative (10008463 Manitoba Inc.) said the change was recommended to avoid future variances.
notes: The second-reading vote and the related rezoning (R18-250, unanimous) were the last decisions of the 2014-2018 council on this file.

title: Annexed Park Road West resident paid the garbage levy for months without pickup
summary: At the hearing to renew the curbside garbage levy (By-law 2111), a resident of land annexed from the RM of Hanover in January 2018 said she was billed the $133 levy for 2018 but got no pickup until September, and asked for a credit. The mayor said the complaint was separate from the by-law and left it with administration to follow up.
status_detail: Referred to administration for follow-up with a letter promised; no public result (credit or explanation) appears in later minutes or transcripts. The levy by-law itself passed.
figures: Levy $133 per residence in 2018, rising $4 a year to $145 in 2021 (City Manager, transcript 0:05:25); E.P. said collection started after Labour Day 2018 (transcript 0:07:15).
reasons: study-first: Said the refund request had nothing to do with the levy by-law being voted on and should be handled separately by administration. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: E.P., Park Road West (annexed 2018), said she attended the annexation meetings, was told garbage and recycling pickup would come, paid the levy and hauled her own garbage to the landfill at $10 a visit until September 2018. Two other residents objected to the flat levy as unfair to small households.
notes: Name of resident reduced to initials. Whether a credit was given is not recorded in any minutes found.

title: Older streets renewed as local improvements: Elmdale (2019), Kroeker (2020), Brandt (2021)
summary: Council used local improvement plans to borrow for rebuilding older streets and their pipes: Elmdale Street (road, 2019), Kroeker Avenue between Main and Third (road, water and sewer, 2020) and Brandt Street (water main and sewer lining, 2021). Brandt was levied on the city-wide water and sewer local improvement districts rather than on frontage owners. Kroeker and Brandt were also put forward for federal-provincial infrastructure grants.
status_detail: All three by-laws passed unanimously with no objectors heard; works were completed and debentures issued (Kroeker By-law 2167, Brandt By-law 2194 in Feb 2022 at 2.42%).
figures: Elmdale: up to $1,050,000 (R19-040). Kroeker: ICIP application total $2.93M, city share $781,431 (R19-177); borrowing up to $2.21M (Municipal Board Order E-20-019, transcript 2020-03-03 0:54:37); tender $1,797,432 (R20-052). Brandt: ICIP application $5.21M, city share $1,389,507 (R19-178); project $2.415M, $1.25M debt, balance from utility funds (transcript 2020-12-15 0:34:38).
public: One letter for and one against the Brandt plan (minutes 2020-12-15).
mover: various (Zwaagstra, Siemens, D. Penner, J. Hiebert)
notes: Kroeker (Dec 17, 2019) and Elmdale (Dec 18, 2018) hearings had no objectors; the Dec 17, 2019 video is missing, so how the Kroeker levy was apportioned (frontage or mill rate) was not confirmed. These are older central streets, included because the topic scope covers local improvements and who pays.

title: Street lights added street by street as new subdivision phases open
summary: Throughout the term council amended the Manitoba Hydro street-lighting contract to light new subdivision streets once built, with the city paying the annual operating cost: Windsor Gate, York Crescent and Acorn; Harmony Lane; Imperial Crescent; Winston Place; Woodhaven Avenue; Prairie Crescent; Wyndham Estate Drive; Malibu, Alpine and Murano; Rosebrook Trail and Caribou; Harmony Lane, Bentley and Carrera; Langill Way and neighbouring Penn-Co streets; Acres Drive; Essex Drive and Sesame Street; McKenzie Avenue; and Park Road West.
status_detail: All approved unanimously as routine resolutions.
figures: Examples: 11 lights on Windsor Gate/York/Acorn, $1,821.60 a year (R19-104); 31 lights on Langill Way area, $5,472.12 a year (R22-148); 12 on Acres Drive, $1,416.96 (R22-149); 16 on Essex/Sesame, $2,824.32 (R22-150).
notes: Routine items grouped. Resolution for Windsor Gate/York/Acorn lights is R19-104 (Apr 16, 2019).

title: Deerfield detention pond and pathway built with city reserves
summary: Council awarded the 2019 Deerfield Middle detention pond and pathway project to Friesen Hauling and Excavating, the low bid. Deerfield, like Clearspring Greens, is a low-service (rural residential) area; this pathway and pond were paid from the city's capital development reserve and gas tax reserve, not by a local levy.
status_detail: Tender awarded unanimously; Siemens said the project came in over $120,000 under budget. Completion was not separately reported in the transcripts searched.
figures: Tender $588,550 plus taxes; 7 bids (R19-064; transcript 0:31:57). Funded from capital development reserve and gas tax reserve (City Manager, 0:31:57).

title: Council objects to rural-residential lots on the RM of Hanover side of the boundary
summary: The RM of Hanover proposed redesignating a quarter section just west of the joint boundary (west of Homestead Crescent) from agriculture to rural residential. On the City Manager's advice, council formally objected, saying unserviced rural lots on the city's edge would block orderly urban growth and future sewer routes.
status_detail: Objection to Hanover Development Plan By-law 2437-19 and Zoning By-law 2438-19 sent (R19-083, unanimous). Hanover's final decision is not in the city record.
reasons: wait-for-development: Lots that cannot be served by city sewer and water impede the urban area's growth. (Mayor Earl Funk); wait-for-development: Rural development leapfrogging the boundary conflicts with provincial land-use policy on eventually connecting to city services. (Susan Penner)
notes: A third speaker (label A, likely the seconder) is not quoted because the identification is not certain.

title: City Manager states the drainage rule for all new development
summary: Asked at a rezoning hearing whether a new apartment site would worsen drainage on a nearby street, the City Manager stated the rule applied to all development: each developer must manage its own water on site and runoff may be no greater or faster than before development. Council members said the details are set in the development agreement before construction.
status_detail: A standing requirement, applied through development agreements and lot grading plans; the agreements themselves are not published with agendas or minutes.
reasons: standards-met: Runoff from a developed site may not exceed pre-development rates; the developer manages its own water. (Troy Warkentin (staff))
public: A neighbour asked whether the project would make drainage on Home Street better, worse or the same.
notes: The site was an infill lot (126 Maplewood Street), not a new subdivision; included only for the statement of the city-wide standard.

title: Clearspring Greens residents demand a safe walkway out of their low-service subdivision
summary: About 100-150 Clearspring Greens residents came with a delegation asking for a pathway out of the subdivision, which has ditches, wells and low-pressure sewer and no sidewalks. They said Old Tom Road and Park Road East had become dangerous after Old Tom was paved. The mayor said council was working on a plan in private because land had to be bought, and the 2019 budget had no room.
status_detail: Led to the 2020 local improvement plan (later cancelled) and to the pathway built in 2021 under a revised 50/50 plan (see 2021-clearspring-pathway-built).
figures: About 140 houses, roughly $48 million in assessed value according to a delegate (transcript 1:21:58).
reasons: cost: The 2019 budget had no room for the work. (Mayor Earl Funk); study-first: A plan was being prepared privately (land purchase) for a study session later in the year. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: M.F. (delegation lead) and other residents said children could not safely bike or walk to school, the park or the pool, that candidates had promised the walkway, and that the neighbourhood paid full taxes. One resident said a child would have to be hurt before action came.
notes: Minutes record about 100 people with the delegation; residents said 140-150. Other speakers identified only by initials or not named.

title: Side-yard variance refused in new Lexington Village to protect the drainage swale
summary: An owner in the new Lexington Village subdivision asked to build a garage 1 foot from the side lot line instead of 4. Staff and the city engineer warned this would interfere with the common swale between houses and raise the risk of overland flooding. Council refused the variance; Siemens's motion to allow 2 feet found no seconder.
status_detail: Variance V-2019-19 denied 5-1 (R19-158).
figures: Required side yard 4 ft; eaves no closer than 2 ft (City Manager, 0:09:49).
reasons: standards-met: Staff and the engineer flagged drainage risk; ignoring it leaves problems for future councils. (Michael Zwaagstra); standards-met: Narrow side yards push one property's water onto another, and the new area's drainage is untested. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: The applicants (S.B. and M.B.) wanted room for a truck-repair garage. M.G., a resident elsewhere, objected from her own experience of a neighbour's encroachment.

title: Lexington Village parks-and-recreation land moved with the relocated detention pond
summary: Goldmark Developments relocated the Lexington Village detention pond to the northwest corner of its land and asked to rezone the original parks-and-recreation (PR) area to residential. Council agreed, on the explanation that the PR land was being moved, not reduced.
status_detail: By-law 2126 given first (R19-171), second (R19-190) and third (R19-191) readings unanimously; the next Lexington phase (Kensington Drive) was approved the same night (R19-192).
reasons: already-planned: Not a reduction of parkland, only a relocation that follows the pond. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No objectors.
seconder: Jake Hiebert; Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert
notes: Whether the PR area after rezoning equals the original area was not stated in figures and was not verified.

title: Residential capital development fees, including a sidewalk levy on new lots, renewed
summary: Council passed By-law 2127 setting residential capital development fees charged on new lots, including a sidewalk levy. In debate, members explained that new-subdivision lots pay this fee up front so sidewalks can be added later, while low-service areas such as Clearspring Greens never paid it.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously in three readings (R19-214, R19-224, R19-225). The 2021 sidewalk fee was $1,610 per single-family dwelling.
figures: Sidewalk portion $1,610 per single-family dwelling in 2021 (City Manager, 2021-01-05 0:34:58). Other fee amounts not checked (no package for Nov 2019 in the project).
reasons: developer-pays: New lots pay toward sidewalks on frontages designed for paths to be installed later. (Damian Penner)
seconder: Damian Penner; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert
notes: The Nov 5 and Nov 19, 2019 meetings were not transcribed (videos missing); decision taken from the minutes.

title: Clearspring Greens pathway proposed as a local improvement with residents paying about 80%
summary: Council held the hearing on By-law 2132: an 850 m, 3 m-wide asphalt pathway with lighting and fencing along Park Road East and from Ramsgate to Fairway Close, with the 146 benefiting parcels paying the $625,000 cost and the city paying for the lot it bought (about $120,000). Residents packed the hearing and objected to the cost. Siemens and Jake Hiebert proposed a cheaper limestone path without lights; that failed 2-5, and the plan passed first and second reading 5-2.
status_detail: 78 objections then went to the Municipal Board; council cancelled this plan on Jan 5, 2021 (R21-011) and replaced it with a 50/50 plan (see 2021-clearspring-plan-revised).
figures: $625,000 project; $4,280.82 per parcel up front or $1,044.05 a year for 5 years at a 7% maximum rate; 146 parcels (minutes 6.2-6.3; transcript 0:09:47-0:11:07). Breakdown per D. Penner: asphalt $270,000, fencing $78,000, lighting $208,000, other $69,000 (1:26:09). City lot purchase about $120,000 (0:15:48). Hespeler-Deerfield pathway (2010-11) cost about $650,000 from city reserves plus a $167,000 federal grant (0:13:21).
reasons: residents-pay-local-improvement: Council's view was that the neighbourhood gets most of the benefit and should pay most of the cost. (Troy Warkentin (staff)); residents-pay-local-improvement: A connecting path for one neighbourhood, requested by it, not part of a wider network; city pays about 20% through the lot. (Damian Penner); fairness-precedent: Not willing to raise what everyone else pays; gas tax was already committed to citywide asphalt overlay. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: An unusually expensive retrofit because the area was never designed for a path. (Michael Zwaagstra); developer-pays: The rural-residential service model never required the developer to build sidewalks or pathways. (Troy Warkentin (staff))
public: S.J. and other residents said low-service lots sold at full market value, Deerfield (also low-service) got a city-paid pathway, gas tax or provincial grants could have helped, and earlier councils' approvals caused the gap. Others objected to the route behind golf-course lots, the fence, break-in risk without lights, and resale effects. Minutes list 26 objectors heard.
vote: 5-2 (against: Jac Siemens, Jake Hiebert); amendment defeated 2-5
notes: Speaker labels in this file merge several residents with council members in places; only turns tied to a named member by the chair or the minutes are used. The fence was proposed as a 10-foot chain-link fence (0:19:42).

title: Council moves the pathway lighting cost to the city, cutting residents' share to about $2,850
summary: Two weeks after the hearing, council voted to take the $208,000 lighting cost out of the local improvement and pay it from the capital development reserve, moving the split to about 45% city and 55% neighbourhood. The objection period to the Municipal Board stayed open.
status_detail: Superseded: the plan still drew 78 objections at the Municipal Board and was cancelled Jan 5, 2021. The pathway finally built in 2021 had no lighting component.
figures: Lighting $208,000 (Zwaagstra, 0:07:01); per-parcel cost from about $4,300 to about $2,800 (0:07:01; City Manager put it at about $2,850 on Jan 5, 2021); about $570 a year (D. Penner, 0:11:40); 32 objections at the time (0:14:30).
reasons: residents-pay-local-improvement: Neighbourhood still pays a significant share of a neighbourhood-requested project, the city a significant part. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Siemens's reason for voting against is not in the transcript; it may reflect his view that residents should pay less still, but that is not recorded.

title: Bush Farm Road neighbour asks when the gravel road will be upgraded as Park Hill grows
summary: At the Park Hill Phase 2 hearing (Sincerus), a Bush Farm Road resident objected that the gravel road, which turns to mud in spring, carries growing traffic from the southwest. The City Manager said developers only improve roads their land fronts, and Park Hill's accesses were on McKenzie Avenue, so no Bush Farm upgrade was required. Council approved the phase and members said peripheral roads should be studied.
status_detail: Park Hill Phase 2 approved unanimously (R20-046 to R20-050). Susan Penner asked for it at the July 2020 study session; in Aug 2021 council widened Bush Farm Road's right-of-way for utilities and drainage (see 2021-bush-farm-widening) but no paving plan was found in this period.
reasons: developer-pays: Developers improve roads fronting their development; Park Hill does not front Bush Farm Road. (Troy Warkentin (staff)); wait-for-development: Development prompts the review of road improvements. (Troy Warkentin (staff)); standards-met: Council must judge the file under the by-laws as written. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: G.H., who lives and runs a business on Bush Farm Road, said the road has no base, carries traffic from Southland Church and Lexington Village, and registered objections to the rezoning, repeal by-law and subdivision.
seconder: Damian Penner; Susan Penner; Damian Penner
notes: No study-session outcome on Bush Farm Road is in the public record.

title: Acres Drive extended to Keating Road as a frontage local improvement despite a charity's objection
summary: To open more industrial lots, council proposed building Acres Drive and its water main from Industrial Road to Keating Road as a local improvement charged by frontage to the two owners: the city's Steinbach Community Development Corporation and Envision Community Living (Eastman Recycling Services). Envision objected that the road gave it no benefit and would cut services. Council proceeded, citing Envision's 2007 development agreement to pay its share of paving and the precedent of never exempting a property. The Municipal Board approved the by-law with an amendment.
status_detail: First reading 5-1 (Siemens against); second reading Apr 20, 2021; Municipal Board hearing Sep 9, 2021 (Order 21E8-0029, approved subject to an amendment); third reading as amended Feb 15, 2022 (R22-044); construction tender $1,645,544.40 Apr 5, 2022 (R22-078); 12 street lights Jun 7, 2022 (R22-149).
figures: Borrowing up to $3.1M (transcripts 2020-12-15 0:06:32; 2022-02-15 0:33:08); Envision's share $102,876, about $20,000 a year over 5 years, corner lot at 50% (Zwaagstra, 2020-12-15 0:24:45); Envision said up to $250,000 (0:08:39).
reasons: fairness-precedent: The city has never carved a property out of a local improvement; doing so would create case-by-case exemptions. (Michael Zwaagstra); developer-pays: Envision's 2007 development agreement committed it to pay its frontage share of paving by local improvement levy. (Michael Zwaagstra); residents-pay-local-improvement: Levies are based on land, not what is built on it. (Susan Penner)
public: J.D. (Envision executive director) and J.D. (Envision board president) said the charity would have to cut staff hours or services, was not consulted before notice was sent during a pandemic code red, and uses only Industrial Road access. A letter from its lawyer objected. Envision Community Living is named as an organization.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Susan Penner; Damian Penner; Susan Penner
vote: first reading 5-1 (against: Jac Siemens; Damian Penner absent); later readings unanimous
notes: The content of the Municipal Board's amendment was not stated in the transcript or minutes and was not verified. Two Envision speakers share the initials J.D. This is an industrial, not residential, extension.

title: Council cancels the Clearspring plan and adopts a 50/50 split capped at the $1,610 sidewalk fee
summary: With 78 of 146 parcels objecting at the Municipal Board, Susan Penner moved to cancel By-law 2132 and start again: no lighting, the asphalt path split 50/50 between residents and city, residents' share capped at $1,610 per parcel (the sidewalk capital development fee charged on new lots), and the lot purchase paid by the city. Both motions passed unanimously.
status_detail: By-law 2132 cancelled (R21-011) and third reading formally denied Feb 16, 2021 (R21-031); new plan drafted as By-law 2168.
figures: 78 objections of 146 parcels (City Manager, 0:33:15); prior per-parcel cost about $2,850 (0:34:03); 2021 sidewalk capital development fee $1,610 per single-family dwelling under By-law 2127 (0:34:58); Penner's estimate: $463,000 without lights, half $231,000, about $1,600 per parcel over 5 years (0:35:38).
reasons: fairness-precedent: $1,610 equals what buyers of new lots already pay for sidewalks, a fee never collected in Clearspring Greens. (Susan Penner); fairness-precedent: The same capital development fee everyone buying a lot has paid for 14 years makes the cost 'sellable'. (Jac Siemens)

title: Revised Clearspring Greens pathway approved, built in 2021 and financed
summary: The new local improvement (By-law 2168) drew only a handful of objections, was approved by the Municipal Board on April 6, 2021, given third reading, and built in the 2021 capital works program. Sixty owners prepaid their share, so the city borrowed $136,850 instead of $233,450.
status_detail: Built in 2021; debenture By-law 2195 given third reading Feb 15, 2022 (R22-046). Members reported the path well used.
figures: Project about $650,000; borrowing proposed $233,450, actual $136,850 at 2.42% over 5 years; residents pay 50% to a maximum $1,610 per parcel (transcripts 2021-02-16 0:09:21, 2022-02-15 0:36:18); 7 written objections at the hearing (mayor, 0:14:23); 2021 capital works tender incl. pathway $1,398,366 (R21-077); 60 prepayments (2021-12-21 0:33:26).
public: One resident at the Feb 16, 2021 hearing withdrew his objection after hearing the lower cost.
seconder: Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert
notes: Earlier report quoted the Feb 15, 2022 turns at 0:36:18 (2178s) and 0:38:02 (2282s); kept here with full fields. The 2021 tender figure covers the whole capital works program, not just the pathway.

title: West-side Brandt Street sidewalk dropped from 2021 tender for cost, then built in the 2022 program
summary: Bids for the Brandt Street (PTH 12) water and sewer renewal came in over budget. On staff advice council deleted the one-block west-side sidewalk (Ellis to Woodhaven Avenue) and added $300,000 from the utility reserve. The sidewalk was included in the 2022 capital works contract awarded in March 2022.
status_detail: Deferred in 2021; 'sidewalks along Branch [Brandt] Street' were part of the $2,083,853 2022 capital works award (R22-053).
figures: Water/sewer tender $2,342,325 plus $300,000 from utility reserve; project budget $2.715M (R21-065; transcript 0:38:13).
reasons: cost: Bids over budget; sidewalk could be re-tendered when prices were better. (Michael Zwaagstra); already-planned: A sidewalk already exists on the east side of the highway. (Susan Penner)

title: Bush Farm Road widened and Park Hill public reserve created for stormwater ponds
summary: Council passed By-law 2181 to widen the Bush Farm Road right-of-way (McKenzie Avenue to half a mile north) for major utilities and to create a public reserve for Park Hill Phase 2 stormwater storage ponds.
status_detail: Three readings unanimous (R21-167, R21-168, R21-184). This widens the right-of-way; it is not a paving project.
figures: Road widening about 50 ft (City Manager, 2021-08-03 0:15:40).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Jake Hiebert

title: Final Hampton Village phase approved over residents' objections about traffic, one access and missing sidewalks
summary: Stonebridge Development Corporation's final 33-lot phase, extending Wyndham Estate Drive (Canterbury Cove) with a public reserve and a future path to the Deerfield pathway, drew objections from Wyndham Estate Drive residents. They cited heavy construction traffic, children walking to the bus with no sidewalks, and 128 lots on a single access although city guidance calls for a second access above 120. The city planner said the 120-lot rule is a flexible policy for emergencies and water-main breaks, and that 2022 capital works would add some sidewalks, with the rest of Wyndham Estate Drive unscheduled. Council gave second reading; objections sent it to the Municipal Board, which imposed no conditions, and third reading followed in May 2022.
status_detail: Phase approved (R21-176, R21-177; R22-129 after Municipal Board hearing Mar 16-17, 2022). Some Wyndham Estates sidewalks were in the 2022 capital works (R22-053); the rest of Wyndham Estate Drive was not scheduled; no second access or construction route was required.
figures: 33 lots; 128 lots past Ashford Lane on one access vs. 120-lot guideline (resident 0:35:04; planner 0:42:04); concept plan approved 2009 (planner 0:33:28).
reasons: already-planned: Consistent with the concept plan approved about 15 years earlier; neighbourhoods should be completed. (Michael Zwaagstra); standards-met: The 120-lot access limit is a flexible policy, not a traffic rule; streets are designed to national guidelines. (Lacey Gaudet (staff)); wait-for-development: Sidewalks will be added through future budgets; the city is growing fast. (Mayor Earl Funk); cost: Further sidewalks could not come before the 2023 budget. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: R.C., A.B., E.B. and C.H., Wyndham Estate Drive and nearby residents, objected: construction traffic and parking, speeding, school-bus access, no sidewalks, and lots pre-sold before approval. R.C. asked for a temporary construction road to Loewen Boulevard and for two entrances before the phase. C.P., for the developer, said parking pressure would ease as other lots were built.
resolution_no: R21-176 (2nd), R21-177 (subdivision), R22-057 (Municipal Board delegation), R22-129 (3rd)
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Damian Penner; Bill Hiebert; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner
notes: Residents and the developer's representative identified by initials. Wyndham Estate Drive sidewalk additions after Oct 2022 are outside this period.

title: Penn-Co development west of Clearspring Mall approved with about 16 acres of parks and trails
summary: Council approved the OCP amendment, rezoning and 139-lot subdivision for a 68-acre Penn-Co Construction development off Park Road West, presented by HTFC Planning and Design as a complete community with a central lake/retention pond, a recreation park with playgrounds, tennis and soccer, walking paths linked to Blind Creek trails, and upgrades to its Park Road West frontage. No one objected. A revised plan (fewer cul-de-sacs, one multifamily parcel) was approved in December 2021.
status_detail: Approved unanimously subject to a development agreement (R21-174, R21-175, R21-224, R21-271). Delivery of the parks was not reported in this period; timing is set in the unpublished development agreement.
figures: 68 acres; 139 residential parcels and 2 public reserves; about 16 acres of parks, more than 23% of the site (applicant, 0:07:37). Park Road West lights approved Aug 16, 2022: 7 x 90 W and 8 x 60 W (R22-197).
public: A.C. (HTFC Planning and Design, for Penn-Co) said parkland exceeded development-plan requirements. A neighbouring owner's architect asked about a future road connection.
resolution_no: R21-174 (subdivision), R21-175 and R21-224 (rezoning), R21-271 (revised subdivision)
mover: Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner
seconder: Bill Hiebert; Damian Penner; Jake Hiebert; Jake Hiebert
notes: Applicant representative identified by initials as a member of the public; companies named.

title: Concrete-bottom swale in Harmony Lane left to the developer, not made a city requirement
summary: At the hearing for Harmony Lane Phase 11 (37 larger lots), a letter from a Hespeler Street neighbour asked whether the developer would install a concrete-bottom swale. The applicant's agent said it would follow whatever the engineers required. Asked whether the swale would be in the development agreement, the City Manager said it was not a city requirement in the previous phase; the developer had installed it voluntarily. Council approved the rezoning, subdivision and variance without adding a condition.
status_detail: Approved unanimously (R21-217 to R21-220) with no swale condition; the drainage design was left to the development agreement and engineers.
figures: 37 lots; residual parcel 11.97 acres vs. 20-acre DR-1 minimum (City Manager, 0:06:22).
reasons: standards-met: A concrete-bottom swale is not a city requirement. (Troy Warkentin (staff)); developer-pays: Phase follows an established neighbourhood; let it move to completion. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: A letter from a neighbour on Hespeler Street raised the swale; D.B., agent for the developer, said it would comply with engineers' requirements.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
seconder: Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Jake Hiebert
notes: The councillor who asked the swale question (label F) is not identified with certainty and is not named.

title: Two-lot split on unserviced Hespeler Street South land refused to avoid more wells and septic
summary: Owners of a 6.75-acre Development Reserve property at 524 Hespeler Street South, served by a private well and septic field, asked to split off a 2-acre house lot. Staff recommended denial. Council refused, saying it would leapfrog development, invite more private wells and septic fields inside the city, and make it costly to extend services later.
status_detail: Denied unanimously (R21-238). Owners must wait for serviced development to reach the area.
figures: 6.75 acres; proposed 2-acre and 4.75-acre lots; DR-1 minimum 20 acres (City Manager 0:19:03; Siemens 0:20:32).
reasons: wait-for-development: Development reserve land must develop incrementally with city water and sewer; no leapfrogging. (Jac Siemens); cost: 2-acre lots make it very expensive to bring services across their frontage to later development. (Damian Penner)
public: The owners (H.K. and E.K.) applied through an agent; they did not speak in the recording.

title: Lexington Village final phase reaches Bush Farm Road; drainage pond built for the whole development
summary: Council approved Goldmark Developments' 62-lot final phase (Essex Drive extension, Sesame Street), subject to a development agreement, a buffer easement and partial closure of a drain. Jake Hiebert raised a recurring culvert problem at the Bush Farm Road corner; the developer's agent said the retention pond was built for the whole development and new rules allow no more runoff than the field produced.
status_detail: Approved unanimously (R22-033); 16 street lights on Essex Drive and Sesame Street approved Jun 7, 2022 (R22-150). The Bush Farm Road culvert issue was raised but no action was recorded.
figures: 62 residential lots (Zwaagstra, 0:11:55).
reasons: standards-met: Runoff cannot exceed pre-development levels; pond over-built for early phases. (D.B. (developer's agent))
public: D.B., agent for Goldmark Developments, answered drainage questions.

title: 2022 capital works add sidewalks on Brandt Street, McKenzie Avenue and in Wyndham Estates
summary: Council awarded the 2022 capital works contract, which included sidewalks on Brandt Street, McKenzie Avenue and in Wyndham Estates (Hampton Village), the area where residents had asked for sidewalks in August 2021. In June council added street lights for the new McKenzie Avenue sidewalk.
status_detail: Contract awarded (R22-053); McKenzie lights approved Jun 21, 2022 (R22-158). Only part of Wyndham Estate Drive was covered; more sidewalk there came in later years (outside this period).
figures: Contract $2,083,853 plus taxes, 3 bids (R22-053; transcript 0:59:59). McKenzie lights: 5 x 90 W, $974.40 a year (R22-158).
notes: 'Branch Street' is the transcript's rendering of Brandt Street. Reused from the existing report (Mar 1, 2022 capital works).

title: Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard subdivision approved; residents' dust, drainage and green-space concerns heard
themes: paving; drainage; parks; sidewalks; annexed; residents; development-agreement
summary: Council gave second reading to the OCP amendment and rezonings and approved the subdivision for a mixed-use development on land annexed in 2018 at Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard, all subject to a development agreement. The applicant promised Loewen Boulevard frontage upgrades with curbing, paving and sidewalks. Loewen Boulevard residents raised dust from the gravel road, drainage, construction traffic and a first phase with no green space. On Oct 4 council rescinded second reading of one rezoning by-law (2213) because of an error in the public notice.
status_detail: Approved unanimously Sep 6 (R22-201 to R22-205), but the subdivision was conditional on By-law 2213, whose second reading was rescinded Oct 4, 2022 (R22-227) for re-notice. The matter continued into the next term.
reasons: wait-for-development: Roads are improved after development comes; phasing follows demand. (Mayor Earl Funk); private-property: Recent drainage problems came from residents over-landscaping, not engineering errors. (Mayor Earl Funk); standards-met: Phasing must be what is efficient; mixing densities phase by phase does not make sense. (Susan Penner)
public: J.C. and other Loewen Boulevard residents said dust was severe all summer, asked how far Loewen would be paved and for pedestrian access to Old Tom, and asked council to require a share of promised amenities in phase 1. C.M., for the applicant, promised frontage upgrades. R.F. (Loewen Boulevard at Old Tom Road) opposed the by-laws, saying his and his neighbours' yards could not handle more runoff.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Susan Penner; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Susan Penner; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner
notes: Quotes at 649, 1463, 1474, 3433, 4109, 4334 and 4493 seconds reused from the existing 2022-2026 report. Jac Siemens's Deerfield-drain question (label D, 0:45:51) is summarized, not quoted.

title: Acres Drive extension paid by frontage levies; $3.1M borrowing cancelled
summary: Acres Drive in the industrial park was built in 2022 as a city-initiated local improvement. In December 2022 the City Manager reported that frontage levies invoiced to the landowner, the Steinbach Community Development Corporation (SCDC), would cover the cost, so council cancelled $3.1M of borrowing authority (By-law 2219) and approved a 4-lot subdivision along the new road.
status_detail: By-law 2219 given first reading Dec 6, 2022 to cancel the borrowing; subdivision 4451-2022-8732 (4 industrial lots of 1.5 acres) approved the same night. The SCDC later created more lots south of Acres Drive (August Cove, Jan 21, 2025, R25-012).
figures: $3.1M borrowing authority cancelled; cost recovered by frontage levies invoiced to the landowner (transcript Dec 6, 2022, 0:18:12).
reasons: developer-pays: The road was charged back to the benefiting landowner through frontage levies, so no city debt was needed. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: No public comment recorded.
resolution_no: not available (no minutes on file for Dec 6, 2022)
notes: Industrial land, not a residential neighbourhood; included for who-pays context. No speaker map for Dec 6, 2022; mover of the By-law 2219 motion could not be identified without minutes.

title: Barkman Avenue and Penner Street renewal paid from city borrowing and reserves
summary: Council used a local improvement plan (By-law 2222) to borrow $1.12M toward street and underground renewal of Barkman Avenue and Penner Street, an older area, with the rest from city reserves. No frontage levy on the owners was mentioned; councillors called it routine renewal.
status_detail: First and second readings Jan 3, 2023 (R23-010, R23-011); third reading Mar 21, 2023 (R23-055); tender with the asphalt overlay program awarded to Maple Leaf Construction for $3,445,402 (R23-058). Debt issue By-law 2240 for $1.12M followed (Dec 19, 2023; Mar 5, 2024).
figures: Estimated cost $2.6M; $1.12M borrowed over 5 years at up to 8%, remainder from reserves (transcript Jan 3, 2023, 0:16:04); combined tender $3,445,402 (minutes R23-058).
public: No one spoke at the Jan 3, 2023 hearing; no written correspondence.
mover: Susan Penner (first and third readings); Damian Penner (second); Michael Zwaagstra (tender)
seconder: Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens

title: City pays to finish paving Park Road West to Industrial Road instead of waiting for development
summary: A developer-led project (Penco) was paving part of Park Road West. Council awarded a $1.97M tender to extend the hard surface about 260 metres to Industrial Road, using reserves, so the gravel gap would not wait for more development. Councillors said residents had asked many times for the road to be paved.
status_detail: Tender awarded to Friesen Hauling Ltd. (R23-057). Phase 1 was complete by summer 2023 and the road was expected to reopen after Oct 13, 2023 (City Manager, Sept 19, 2023).
figures: $1,970,097 plus taxes; other bids from $2,125,645 (minutes R23-057); about 260 metres left to pave (mayor, transcript 0:52:21).
reasons: wait-for-development: Normally paving follows development ('developer-driven system'); healthy reserves let the city finish the road now instead of waiting. (Damian Penner)
public: The mayor said residents had asked many times in meetings in his office for the road to be paved.

title: Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard development: approved 2022, still waiting on the Manning Canal in 2026
summary: After the Sept 2022 hearing where neighbours raised dust, drainage and green space, council gave third readings to the plan and zoning changes (June 2023) and a plan of drain for the Manning Canal through the site (June 2023). The subdivision approval then neared expiry because the drain needed provincial agreement; in Feb 2026 council re-approved it subject to a revised development agreement, and in July-Aug 2026 passed a plan of works for the canal segment.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2211 and rezonings 2212/2213 third reading Jun 6, 2023 (R23-115 to R23-117); plan of drain By-law 2228 first and second readings Jun 20, 2023 (R23-127, R23-128); subdivision 4451-2022-8586 re-approved Feb 3, 2026 subject to a revised development agreement (R26-030); plan of works By-law 2227 Jul 21 and Aug 4, 2026 (R26-152, R26-160, R26-161). No record that lots, paving or green space promised in 2022 had been delivered by Nov 2026.
figures: Approval period: subdivision approvals last 2 years plus a 1-year extension (City Manager, Feb 3, 2026, 0:26:10).
reasons: wait-for-development: The project was held up by the Manning Canal and the public reserve along it, which needed an agreement with the province (MTI). (Jac Siemens)
public: At the Sept 2022 hearing (previous period) R.F. of Loewen Boulevard objected over flooding and asked for a retention pond; J.C. raised dust and the lack of green space in the first phase.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R23-115); Damian Penner (R23-116, R23-127); Jac Siemens (R23-117, R26-030, R26-152); Jake Hiebert (R26-160); Bill Hiebert (R26-161)
notes: File 4451-2022-8586 is the Sept 6, 2022 subdivision on Loewen Boulevard (R22-204); the 2022 minutes record R.F. of 435 Loewen Boulevard objecting to it. Whether By-law 2228 received third reading was not found in the 2023 minutes searched.

title: Hampton Village: park built with neighbours' help; stop sign and crosswalk by the new playground refused
summary: A Hampton Village resident had asked since Aug 2022 for a 3-way stop at Wyndham Estate Drive and Ashford Lane near the new park and middle school. Staff counts did not support it and council refused, adding a no-stopping zone instead. The park itself had been planned as passive green space; neighbours worked with the city to add a play structure and a picnic shelter, and council named it Chris Goertzen Park.
status_detail: Stop sign refused and no-stopping zone added (R23-125, 6-1, S. Penner against); the mayor asked to revisit it once the area was built out, with no later decision found. Park play structure installed spring-summer 2023; park named Sept 5, 2023 (R23-183). A pedestrian crossing near the park was not added.
figures: Traffic counts done May 26, 2023 (minutes 10.1); stop-sign wait under 15 seconds (City Manager, 0:25:17).
reasons: standards-met: The city's traffic-control guideline did not warrant a stop sign; revisit when a park access is built. (Jac Siemens); wait-for-development: Bring it back once the area is fully developed and park use is known. (Earl Funk)
public: The original request came from a resident at 46 Wyndham Estate Drive (minutes); Jake Hiebert credited a resident who worked to get the park built.

title: Lot grading plans made a condition of variances, including on older lots
summary: Council repeatedly approved variances only on condition that the owner supply an approved lot grading or site servicing plan, including for older properties built before the city's grading rules and one property for which the city had no grading plan on file. Councillors said owners must manage water on their own site.
status_detail: Conditions attached to V-2023-04 (R23-123), V-2023-10 (R23-149), V-2023-13 (R23-166), V-2024-12 (R24-180), V-2025-05 (R25-058), V-2025-06 (R25-059) and an as-built plan for V-2025-36 (R25-250). In Apr 2026 council approved V-2026-07 for an older house on Kroeker Avenue with a 2.4-foot side yard over the engineering department's objection, relying on a lot grading plan named in the City Manager's recommendation (R26-077, recorded 4-1 with Jake Hiebert against; the resolution text itself lists no condition). Whether the plans were later filed was not reported to council.
reasons: private-property: Owners must manage water on their own site; poor grading on one lot affects how neighbouring lots drain. (Jac Siemens); standards-met: A lot grading plan addresses the engineer's drainage concern, so the variance can be approved. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No objections at these hearings.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R23-123, R23-149, R25-058, R25-250, R26-077); Damian Penner (R23-166); Jac Siemens (R24-180); Susan Penner (R25-059)
vote: unanimous except R26-077, 4-1 as recorded (against: Jake Hiebert); R25-058 vote not recorded in minutes

title: New residential subdivisions approved subject to development agreements, with no service conditions set at council
summary: Council approved a steady run of residential subdivisions, each 'subject to the execution of a development agreement' negotiated by staff, without adding conditions on sidewalks, parks or drainage at the meeting. Examples: 70 lots with three public reserves off McKenzie Avenue (Sterling Crescent, Aug 2023), Agassiz Shore (Nov 2023), Blind Creek Boulevard off Park Road West (Apr 2024), Park Hill/Kootenay Way phase 2B (22 lots, Apr 2024), Park Hill Rosebrook Trail/Pacific Bay (41 lots, Dec 2025) and Williams Creek (153 lots, Aug 2026).
figures: Sterling Crescent subdivision: 70 lots incl. 14 RMD, 12 RLD, 44 single-family and 3 public reserves (Siemens, Aug 1, 2023, 0:22:13).
reasons: standards-met: Applications consistent with the zoning by-law and OCP are approved; details go into the development agreement. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: At the Sterling Crescent hearing N.T. (Coral Crescent) asked about lots backing onto hers and said runoff becomes everybody's problem when lots are packed together; staff answered with setback rules.
mover: Jac Siemens (R23-159); Michael Zwaagstra (R23-238, R24-084, R25-245); Jake Hiebert (R24-074, R26-204); Damian Penner (R26-157)
notes: Commercial and industrial subdivisions in the same period are not listed. 'Astor and Crescent' is the transcript's rendering of Sterling Crescent.

title: Unbuilt First Street back lane closed and kept as a public drain
summary: As a condition of an approved subdivision on First Street, council closed a registered but never-built public lane behind First Street properties and designated it a plan of works, because it has always served as a major drain. A neighbouring landowner objected that he wanted a lane there; staff said building a road over the drain would be cost-prohibitive.
status_detail: By-law 2232 second and third readings carried 5-2 (R23-226, R23-227), fulfilling a condition of subdivision 4451-2022-8794 (R23-143, Jul 4, 2023).
reasons: cost: Keeping the drain working while building a lane over it would be extremely cost-prohibitive. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: A First Street landowner (developer) filed a written objection, wanting the lane for future development access.

title: Annexed rural lots: drainage setback variance refused in 2023, small variance allowed in 2026
summary: On a 4-acre property on PTH 52 West annexed in 2018, staff warned that cutting a side setback from 15 to 4 feet could limit future drainage, and council denied it, with Jake Hiebert noting no drainage plan was provided. In 2026 council approved a smaller side-yard variance on an annexed farmstead on Hanover Road West, with Jac Siemens noting annexed properties came with older rural rules.
status_detail: V-2023-22 denied 5-1 (R23-251, B. Hiebert against). V-2026-17 approved Sep 1, 2026.
figures: Requested side yard 4 ft vs 15 ft required (2023); 10.85 ft vs 15 ft (2026) (transcripts).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Approving a 4-foot setback could set a precedent for neighbouring highway-frontage lots expected to develop. (Jac Siemens)
public: No one spoke at either hearing.
resolution_no: R23-251; V-2026-17 resolution number not in the parsed motions
seconder: Jac Siemens (2023); Susan Penner (2026, per transcript)
vote: 2023: 5-1 (against: Bill Hiebert); 2026: carried, no opposition heard

title: Developer given back donated park land in Hampton Village to make up for lots lost to a temporary turnaround
summary: Stonebridge Development Corporation could not get a neighbour's consent for a temporary turnaround, so three approved lots were used for it. It asked the city to close part of the park land (public reserve) it had donated on Wyndham Estate Drive and turn it into a building lot. Staff said the remaining green space still exceeded the city's minimum. A neighbour asked whom this benefited and raised the single road access; council approved.
status_detail: By-law 2237 first reading Dec 19, 2023 (R23-258); second and third readings Jan 16, 2024 (R24-007, R24-008); related subdivision 4451-2023-8865 approved (R24-018).
figures: Original subdivision was about 31 lots; three lots used for the turnaround; the new lot does not raise the net lot count (City Manager, 0:34:07, 0:40:09).
reasons: standards-met: Even after the closing, the developer had provided more public green space than city policy requires. (Michael Zwaagstra); already-planned: Enough room remains for the planned active transportation route and the Deerfield drain. (Jac Siemens)
public: D.M. (Wyndham Estate Drive) objected, asking whether the change benefited the developer rather than residents, and whether the area's single access was overloaded. P.K. asked about servicing a new lot on a new road and recalled a cap of 120 units on one access.
mover: Susan Penner (R23-258, R24-008, R24-018); Jac Siemens (R24-007)
seconder: Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra

title: Creekside Drive residents on wells object to a truck yard next door; yard denied, wells not addressed
summary: Residents of Creekside Drive and Winston Place objected to a truck yard on Tower Avenue. G.P. said everyone on his street is on private wells near a ditch that takes runoff (and was once a city snow dump), and that dust from city fill work had kept his children indoors. Council denied the conditional use as incompatible with the neighbourhood. No servicing response on the wells was discussed.
status_detail: Conditional use CU-2023-02 denied unanimously (R24-009). The well-water and ditch-runoff concerns were not taken up; the 2025 OCP ban on new private wells applies to new buildings only.
figures: About 17 written objections (minutes 22.2).
reasons: private-property: Only parking stalls must be hard-surfaced; the truck yard itself would be gravel. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: G.P. (Creekside Drive): wells near the runoff ditch, a $5,000 water treatment system, dust. Other neighbours raised children's safety on the walking path to the middle school, noise and lights.

title: City builds sidewalks in Wyndham Estates years after homes went in, paid from city funds
summary: The 2026 capital works program added 320 metres of new sidewalk on Wyndham Estate Drive and a 65-metre link from Winston Place to Deerfield Trail, alongside asphalt resurfacing, funded from the general operating fund, the capital development reserve and the gas tax reserve. A Parkland Drive sidewalk to the new school had been built in 2025.
status_detail: 2026 capital works awarded to Maple Leaf Construction (R26-049). The 2024 program (R24-064, $1,324,707) covered Hanover, Penner and Brandt streets.
figures: 2026 award $1,379,680 plus taxes against a consultant estimate of $1,972,455 (transcript Mar 3, 2026, 0:06:28; minutes R26-049).
reasons: wait-for-development: Sidewalks go in after neighbourhoods are 80%+ built to avoid construction damage (Aug 4, 2026). (Earl Funk)
public: In Aug 2026 G.W. of Wyndham Estate Drive said installing these sidewalks late meant digging up and re-sodding finished yards at taxpayers' expense.

title: Standing-water complaints on Chrysler Gate and Harmony Lane: swales found built to plan, no fix ordered
summary: After a wet spring, G.P. and P.P. of Chrysler Gate wrote about standing water; a Harmony Lane owner followed. Council referred it to staff. Two months later staff reported that the drainage swales in city parkland behind the lots were built to the approved plans and within tolerance, suggested a minor fix on one private lot, and expected the problem to resolve as the ground dried. Council received the report as information.
status_detail: Referred by consensus May 21, 2024; report received as information Jul 16, 2024. No remedial work on the swales; one owner advised to regrade part of a private yard.
reasons: standards-met: Swales were built to the approved plan and verified elevations were within tolerance. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); private-property: The only recommendation was minor surface work on one private lot. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
