public: Letters from G.P. and P.P. (Chrysler Gate) and L.R. and J.R. (Harmony Lane), per the minutes.

title: City adds Hydro street lights for new subdivision streets and pays their yearly cost
summary: As new streets were finished, council amended its Manitoba Hydro street lighting contract to add LED lights and take on their annual operating cost: one on Parkland Drive by the new school (2024), six on Kootenay Way (2025) and 13 in Park Hill Phase 2C (2026). Councillors treated it as routine and part of the citywide street light program.
figures: Annual operating cost: Parkland Drive 1 light $176.52; Kootenay Way 6 lights $1,059.12; Park Hill Phase 2C 13 lights $2,386.80 (minutes). The mayor read the Park Hill figure as '$23,868 per year' (transcript Feb 3, 2026, 0:29:38); the minutes figure is used.
public: None recorded.
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner
notes: Who pays to install the lights (developer or city) was not stated at these meetings.

title: New Official Community Plan: runoff no higher than before development, path links in new areas, no private wells where city water is available
summary: In the 2023-2025 review of the Official Community Plan, council adopted policies that new developments must hold runoff to pre-development levels, must create active transportation connections, and that buildings connected or able to connect to city water may not use private wells. Councillors said the runoff rule was already done in principle.
status_detail: Direction to proceed Dec 3, 2024 (R24-234); first and second readings after the public hearing Apr 1, 2025 (R25-069, R25-070); third reading Sept 16, 2025 (R25-184). The policies cover new development; no plan for existing well and septic areas was discussed.
public: At the Apr 1, 2025 hearing R.J. (near Avondale) asked about the private well rule; the planner said it is in the OCP, not the zoning by-law.
mover: Susan Penner (R24-234, R25-184); Jac Siemens (R25-069); Jake Hiebert (R25-070)
seconder: Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra

title: City objects to Hanover approving businesses on fringe land without Steinbach standards
summary: The RM of Hanover approved a subdivision just north of the city on PTH 12 over Steinbach's objection, issued building permits, and then proposed rezoning the land to rural industrial after businesses were already built. Council filed a formal objection, saying it broke the joint annexation agreement for the transition area and would leave land developed below city standards where Steinbach expects to grow.
status_detail: Objection filed Dec 17, 2024 (R24-246). The rezoning went to the Municipal Board, with the City Manager and City Planner delegated to the August 22, 2025 hearing (R25-163). No outcome was reported to council by Nov 2026.
public: None recorded.

title: Active transportation plan accepted as a guide; about $11M of paths and sidewalks, no funding set
summary: Council accepted the city's first active transportation plan (Urban Systems) as a long-term guide to sidewalks, crossings and multi-use paths. Councillors praised developer-built pathways in Lang Hill Farms and said the plan lets the city reserve path corridors as the edges of the city develop, but stressed high costs and noted residents of established streets have resisted new sidewalks.
status_detail: Accepted May 6, 2025 (R25-096). No implementation budget was adopted with it; Wyndham Estate Drive sidewalks were funded in the 2026 capital works program.
figures: About $11 million in total for all projects (Zwaagstra, 1:03:48); federal Active Transportation Fund covers up to 60% to $5M (consultant, 0:56:58).
reasons: cost: Price tags are very high; most of the plan is far in the future. (Michael Zwaagstra); residents-pay-local-improvement: Sidewalks in established neighbourhoods draw strong opposition (Madison Drive, 2007). (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: None at the meeting; the mayor reported youth asking for pathways linking neighbourhoods.

title: Subdivision relying on easement servicing denied; property had an unanswered drainage work order
summary: Council denied a subdivision at 236 Woodhaven Avenue that would have created lots without frontage on a public street, served by easement, for financing reasons. Councillors cited the city engineer's rule that every parcel be serviced directly from the public right-of-way, and an outstanding 2024 work order for a drainage plan on the property that the owner had not answered.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2024-9057 denied unanimously (R25-109).
figures: Lots of about 14,000 sq ft where 20,000 sq ft required (transcript 0:25:11).
reasons: standards-met: Servicing across private property by easement creates shared obligations and future disputes; city standards require direct public servicing. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Approving exceptions for one developer's financing would invite similar requests. (Susan Penner)
public: The applicant's lawyer argued the subdivision was needed for phased financing.

title: Front-yard variance in a new subdivision approved 4-3 despite the city engineer's stormwater warning
summary: Days after the September 2025 storm, a builder asked to reduce a front yard from 25 to 17 feet on a corner duplex lot in the new Sterling Crescent subdivision. The city engineer recommended denial because larger footprints add runoff beyond what the subdivision's stormwater system was designed for and set a precedent; the City Manager recommended approval. Council approved it 4-3.
status_detail: Variance V-2025-22 approved (R25-177): for Siemens, B. Hiebert, D. Penner, S. Penner; against Funk, J. Hiebert, Zwaagstra.
figures: Front yard 17 ft vs 25 ft required (minutes).
reasons: standards-met: The subdivision's overall design answers the stormwater question; one lot makes little difference. (Jac Siemens)
public: No objectors; the builder's representative said he had not heard of flooding in Lexington Village.
vote: 4-3 (against: Earl Funk, Jake Hiebert, Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Diarization merged the City Manager label C with councillor turns at 0:16:29 and 0:18:05 (likely Jake Hiebert and Damian Penner); those were not quoted.

title: Lot grading policy review listed for the future; Land Drainage By-law adds inspections and fines
summary: After the 2024 and 2025 storms, staff listed possible future projects including a review of the private-property lot grading policy, a drainage catchment master plan and a review of basement depth for new construction. Council passed Land Drainage By-law 2274, replacing the sump pump by-law with rules for private-property stormwater, inspections and fines, with exemptions possible for older homes. A climate risk assessment promised in 2025 as a roadmap for drainage projects was presented in August 2026.
status_detail: By-law 2274 first reading May 19, 2026 (R26-102); second and third Aug 4, 2026 (R26-162, R26-163); penalty schedule By-law 2282 the same night. The lot grading policy review and drainage master plan had no reported start date. Climate adaptation plan presented Aug 18, 2026 (minutes).
figures: Annual programs: sanitary sewer televising just over $100,000, storm sewer about $60,000, major drain maintenance $50,000 (City Manager, Mar 17, 2026, 0:17:48).
reasons: study-first: Lot grading review, drainage master plan and basement depth review are projects that 'could be looked at in the future'. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); private-property: The by-law targets nuisance water and sump pumps on private property. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Jac Siemens relayed residents' request for guidance on where to discharge sump water in shoulder seasons.
mover: Jake Hiebert (R26-102); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-162); Damian Penner (R26-163)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert

title: City takes title to drains running through new subdivisions so it can maintain them
summary: When land with an existing drain is subdivided, the city now has the drain strip transferred to it and designated a plan of works, so the city, not future lot owners, maintains it. Examples: the drain south of Acres Drive in the SCDC's August Cove industrial subdivision (By-law 2267, 2025) and the drain on a 5-acre multi-unit site at 60 McKenzie Avenue (2026), where room was confirmed for the bike path to continue along the drain.
status_detail: By-law 2267 first reading Oct 7, 2025 (R25-190), second and third Nov 4, 2025 (R25-213, R25-214); 60 McKenzie subdivision approved subject to a plan of works by-law and development agreement Jun 2, 2026 (R26-113).
figures: 60 McKenzie site about 5 acres; drain parcel transferred to the city by consent expropriation (City Manager, Jun 2, 2026, 1:17:04).
public: None recorded.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R25-190); Jake Hiebert (R25-213, R26-113); Damian Penner (R25-214)
seconder: Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert

title: Clear Spring Greens: small drainage project and a council-initiated low-pressure sewer reroute; ditches and septic tanks remain
summary: Clear Spring Greens is served by septic tanks feeding a low-pressure sewer that discharges into the Georgetown gravity sewer. After Georgetown residents (M.R.) linked it to repeated backups, council initiated a reroute of the low-pressure line along Park Road East to PTH 12, awarded in July 2026. The city also did a $30,000 drainage project in Clear Spring Greens in 2025. A Granite Park resident said the area still relies on ditches, low-pressure sewer and septic tanks.
status_detail: Reroute tender awarded to Beaver Sewer & Water Services Ltd. (R26-149), to be built in the 2026 season. No plan to replace septic tanks or ditches with full city services was discussed.
figures: Drainage project about $30,000 (City Manager, Mar 17, 2026, 0:17:48); reroute $396,500 vs consultant estimate $614,000 (City Manager, Jul 21, 2026, 1:19:16; minutes R26-149). M.R.'s survey: 39 of 83 homes backed up Sept 17, 2024 and 58 of 83 on Sept 12, 2025 (Oct 21, 2025, 0:18:19).
public: M.R. (Golfview Crescent) presented a door-to-door survey and questioned mixing the low-pressure system into the 1988 gravity sewer; D.J. (Granite Park) said growth was planned before infrastructure.
notes: Sewer-backup aspects are covered in the sewer-backups report; included here for the fringe-servicing angle.

title: Animal rescue asks city to clear a clogged creek off Keating Road; Keating Drain cleaned out by November
summary: M.N., speaking for a not-for-profit animal rescue on Keating Road whose building flooded two years running, said the creek beside it was too shallow and full of brush and asked the city to keep it clear as its public works page promises. The mayor said it would go into the stormwater investigation. In March 2026 the City Manager reported the Keating Drain from PTH 52 West to Park Road West had been cleaned out for about $30,000 by November 2025.
status_detail: Keating Drain cleanout completed Nov 2025 (reported Mar 17, 2026). Whether this is the same channel M.N. described was not stated.
figures: Cleanout about $30,000 (City Manager, Mar 17, 2026, 0:17:48); insurance deductible $25,000 (M.N., Oct 21, 2025, 0:32:52).
public: M.N.: told after both floods that the creek was not the problem and that it was a 1-in-100-year event.

title: City secures strips of land for future sidewalks and walkways when lots redevelop
summary: When owners subdivide or redevelop, the city has taken land for future sidewalks: a road-widening by consent at Friesen Avenue and Elmdale Street (By-law 2269) and a 15-foot no-build strip on McKenzie-area lots that a builder said limited his parking. The mayor said the strip is kept for future infrastructure, whether or not it becomes a walkway.
status_detail: By-law 2269 first reading Oct 21, 2025 (R25-200), second and third Nov 4, 2025 (R25-216, R25-217). The parking variance for the 15-foot-strip project passed 5-2 (R25-222).
figures: 15-foot no-build line (Nov 18, 2025, 0:24:58).
public: The builder's representative (Hillside Custom) said the reserved strip cost parking stalls.
mover: Susan Penner (R25-200); Damian Penner (R25-216); Jake Hiebert (R25-217)
seconder: Bill Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Susan Penner
notes: These are infill and downtown sites rather than new subdivisions.

title: At infill hearings, neighbours' drainage questions are answered with 'the development agreement will deal with it'
summary: At hearings for infill and multi-unit projects (First Street, Dec 2025; Lund/Westview area, Jul 2026; Giesbrecht, Sep 2026), neighbours asked how runoff would be handled, and on Giesbrecht said the street already floods. The mayor answered that drainage is settled in the development agreement between the developer and staff, that each site must hold its own water, and that infill usually improves drainage. Jac Siemens said streets act as collectors in heavy rain because pipes big enough would not be affordable.
status_detail: Projects were approved subject to development agreements (e.g., R25-248, R26-132, R26-179). The 58 Giesbrecht rezoning (By-law 2285) got third reading Oct 20, 2026 (transcript; no minutes on file yet). No street-level drainage fix for Giesbrecht was decided.
reasons: standards-met: Each development must handle its own water through a drainage plan tied to its permit. (Earl Funk); cost: Pipes large enough to carry all water in torrential rain are not financially feasible; streets become collectors. (Jac Siemens)
public: J.W. (Westview Drive) asked how much more runoff would go to the ditch behind his yard; G.W. of Giesbrecht (a different person from the Williams Creek G.W.) said the street is 'almost a river' in heavy rain and paved lots will add to it.
mover: Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Bill Hiebert

title: Park Hill: request for sidewalks on every new street refused; city says sidewalks come later, by design
summary: A written conditional objection to the 41-lot Rosebrook Trail/Pacific Bay phase of Park Hill asked for confirmation that sidewalks or walkways would be built on listed streets. The City Manager said developers are generally not required to build sidewalks, as a deliberate city strategy, and the city adds them later where needed; the answer for the listed streets was no. Council approved the subdivision and rezoning.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2025-9173 approved (R25-245) and By-law 2268 rezoning given second and third readings (R25-246, R25-247) with no sidewalk condition. The Parkland Drive sidewalk to the new school was built in 2025; more were recommended for 2026 or 2027. Park Hill public reserves were realigned in 2026 (By-laws 2278, 2279), with no reserve land lost per staff.
figures: 41 residential lots (Zwaagstra, 0:08:26).
reasons: wait-for-development: Sidewalks are planned but go in after most building is done. (Michael Zwaagstra); standards-met: Bays and crescents commonly have no sidewalks. (Susan Penner); already-planned: A build-out trigger and the active transportation plan will bring sidewalks to streets that need them. (Earl Funk)
public: One written conditional objection from a resident asked for sidewalks/walkways on listed streets; the writer did not attend.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (R25-245); Susan Penner (R25-246); Jake Hiebert (R25-247)
seconder: Susan Penner; Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra

title: Proposed sidewalk condition for McKenzie Avenue apartments not adopted
summary: At the hearing for 48 apartments on McKenzie Avenue, neighbours raised the lack of a sidewalk on the south side and asked who would pay for one. Jac Siemens asked to add sidewalk construction to the development agreement as a friendly amendment; mover Damian Penner declined, saying he is not an engineer. The City Manager said such a requirement should be a condition of approval. No condition was added and the rezoning passed.
status_detail: Second reading of By-law 2273 carried unanimously without a sidewalk condition (R26-068); third reading Sept 1, 2026 (R26-184).
figures: 48 apartments (existing report).
reasons: study-first: Not an engineer; a sidewalk might not be feasible or appropriate, so he would not put it in the agreement. (Damian Penner)
public: P.K. asked who would pay for a south-side sidewalk, saying neighbours had paid for the north-side one as a local improvement; H.H. worried he would have to pay for street or sidewalk work. Neighbours also raised sewer backups and drainage.

title: City signs agreement to take over the Manning Canal from the province
summary: The Manning Canal drains the city's east and north and was the only drain in Steinbach still under full provincial control. After talks since 2022, council approved a memorandum of understanding with Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure so the city can take jurisdiction, saying it would let the city improve the drain and decide faster on development along it.
status_detail: MOU approved Apr 21, 2026 (R26-081). The formal transfer needs a Lieutenant Governor in Council decision, not reported done by Nov 2026. The plan of works for the canal segment at Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard passed Aug 4, 2026.
figures: Negotiations since 2022 (minutes R26-081 item 18).
public: None recorded at this item; Williams Creek neighbours (Aug 4, 2026) raised drainage into the same area.

title: Williams Creek phase 1 (153 lots) approved subject to a development agreement
summary: Council gave second reading to the Williams Creek rezoning and approved the subdivision and road openings south of Loewen Boulevard. The developer said a 30-foot public reserve with a concrete-bottom swale would carry water behind neighbours' lots and that phase 1 would pay a fee instead of park land. Construction access off Loewen Boulevard and improvements to Loewen were left to the development agreement.
status_detail: First reading Jul 7, 2026; second reading Aug 4, 2026 (R26-156); subdivision and road openings approved subject to third reading and a development agreement (R26-157). Third reading was not found in meetings through Oct 20, 2026.
figures: 153 lots in phase 1 on about 74 acres (transcript Aug 4, 2026; Hiebert cited 155 houses); 30-ft concrete-bottom swale (applicant, 0:27:04).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Adding rules at the hearing that go beyond the zoning by-law is unfair to applicants. (Michael Zwaagstra); standards-met: Plan meets the zoning by-law with drainage in place. (Jake Hiebert or Bill Hiebert)
public: See 2026-williams-creek-residents-asks.

title: Residents ask who checks developers' drainage studies; Albert Street back lane promise unanswered
summary: At the July 2026 hearing for a 6-storey seniors building near Stonebridge Crossing, the City Manager read the standard development agreement clauses: the owner pays for utility services and must ensure drainage works and submit a professional lot grading plan before the first building permit. Residents asked for independent review, since the consultants work for the developer. B.K. of Albert Street said a back lane promised to be graded when nearby apartments were built never was; no answer was recorded.
status_detail: The variance was approved 6-1 (R26-147, Siemens against on building height). No independent review of developer studies was adopted, and no response on the Albert Street back lane appears in later meetings to Nov 2026.
reasons: standards-met: Developments meeting the city's design standards and system capacity are generally approved; no system can handle beyond 1-in-100-year rain. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager); developer-pays: Standard clause: the owner pays all utility servicing costs. (Troy Warkentin, City Manager)
public: M.R. and G.R. (Golfview Crescent) asked for third-party review of developer studies; B.K. (Albert Street) raised the ungraded back lane and flooding; D.J. (Granite Park) questioned whether infrastructure kept pace with growth.

title: Williams Creek neighbours ask for drainage first, sidewalks and playgrounds right away; none added as conditions
themes: drainage; sidewalks; playgrounds; parks; residents; development-agreement
summary: Neighbours from Wyndham Estates and Ash Grove Lane asked that drainage be fixed before construction, that walkways and playgrounds be built immediately, to see the engineered drawings and to require concrete driveways and a construction route. The mayor said sidewalks go in after 80%+ build-out, that council does not see or get involved in the development agreement, and that one neighbour's problem seemed isolated to his property. The developer said the first phase would pay a park fee and any park would come in phase 2.
status_detail: No condition on drainage timing, sidewalks, playgrounds or driveways was added (R26-156, R26-157). Existing drainage problems on Wyndham Estate Drive and Ash Grove Lane were not part of the decision; Siemens invited G.W. to speak at the next zoning or development review.
reasons: wait-for-development: Sidewalks go in at 80%+ build-out so construction traffic does not damage them. (Earl Funk); private-property: A neighbour's drainage problem appeared isolated to his own property. (Earl Funk); developer-pays: Green space handled through the development agreement's dedication requirement. (Earl Funk)
public: G.W. (Wyndham Estate Drive, retired land developer): drainage first, walkways and playgrounds immediately, digging up yards for late sidewalks wasted taxpayers' money. S.B. (Ash Grove Lane): drainage problems began when Wyndham was built and no one has a solution. M.J. (William's Creek Development Inc., applicant): driveways and construction routes are the city's to require in the agreement; no playground in phase 1.
